about: Jane's own topics: added by this project, not part of the Marble Skill Taxonomy. Same schema as data/marble/topics.json. Ids start with jane_ (never mt_) so they can never collide with Marble ids, and they live outside data/marble/ so a Marble data refresh never touches them. build.mjs appends them after the Marble topics in public/tax.json. centrality is hand-set (Marble computes its own; the app does not use it). See data/jane/README.md.

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Compound growth
topics.description: Money that earns interest on its interest grows by the same percentage each period: future value = present value × (1 + rate)^years (FV = PV × (1+r)^n); why savings and investments grow along a curve that gets steeper over time, unlike simple interest, which adds the same amount each year
evidence: Work out year by year how $100 grows at 10% a year for 3 years, and explain why each year adds more than the last
Use FV = PV × (1 + r)^n to find the value of a saving after a given number of years
Compare simple and compound interest on the same amount and explain why the compound total pulls ahead
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saved $200 at 5% interest a year, could they work out how much it would be worth after 3 years, and explain why it grows faster each year?

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: The Rule of 72
topics.description: Doubling money with a mental-math shortcut: when money grows by the same percent every year, it takes about 72 ÷ the yearly rate in percent years to double (at 6% a year, about 12 years); a first taste of how savings grow that needs only percentages, before the full compound growth formula; the same rule estimates how fast inflation halves what money can buy
evidence: Explain what it means for money to double (for example $50 growing to $100) and why a higher yearly rate doubles it sooner
Estimate how many years it takes money to double at 6%, 8% and 12% a year using 72 ÷ rate
Work backwards to find the growth rate needed to double money in a given number of years
Use the rule to estimate how long it takes 4% inflation to halve what a dollar buys
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} heard that a savings account pays 9% a year, could they estimate in their head how many years it would take the money to double?

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Real return and inflation
topics.description: Inflation means prices rise over time, so the same money buys less; the real return is what savings grow by after inflation: (1 + rate) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1, roughly the rate minus the inflation rate
evidence: Explain what inflation is, using a price that has gone up over time
Estimate the real return when savings earn 5% and prices rise 3% (about 2%)
Use (1 + r) ÷ (1 + i) − 1 to find the exact real return and compare it with the r − i estimate
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s savings earned 4% in a year when prices rose 6%, could they explain whether they can buy more or less than before, and by roughly how much?

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Present value
topics.description: Money today is worth more than the same amount later, because today's money can grow; present value runs compound growth backwards: PV = FV ÷ (1 + rate)^years, to compare money at different times
evidence: Explain why $100 today is worth more than $100 in five years
Use PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^n to find how much to save now to have a target amount later
Compare two offers paid at different times (for example $100 now or $110 next year) at a given interest rate
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} were offered $100 now or $120 in three years, could they use present value to decide which is the better deal when savings earn 8% a year?

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: True average return (geometric mean)
topics.description: The fair average of yearly growth rates is the geometric mean: multiply the growth factors, take the nth root, then subtract 1; why +50% followed by −50% loses money even though the simple average of the rates is 0%
evidence: Show that $100 up 50% then down 50% ends at $75, and explain why the simple average of 0% is misleading
Turn yearly percentage changes into growth factors (like 1.2 and 0.9) and multiply them
Find the true average yearly return by taking the nth root of the product of the growth factors and subtracting 1
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw an investment go up 20% one year and down 20% the next, could they explain why it did not break even and work out its true average yearly return?

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Profit per customer
topics.description: What one customer is really worth to a business: the money they pay (revenue) minus what it cost to get them (acquisition cost, like flyers or free samples) and to serve them (delivery cost, like cups, lemons or snacks); a business can only grow when each new customer brings in more than they cost (source: FounderOS — designing-money-models)
evidence: Work out the profit from one lemonade customer who pays $3 when the cup and lemons cost $1 and the flyer that brought them cost $1
Name the cost to get a customer and the cost to serve a customer for a snack stand
Explain why selling to more customers loses money if each customer costs more than they pay
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} ran a snack stand, could they work out how much profit one customer brings after the cost of getting and serving them?

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Payback period
topics.description: How many sales (or days) it takes for a customer to pay back what it cost to win them: payback = acquisition cost ÷ profit per sale; the 30-day payback rule: a healthy money model earns back the cost of getting and serving a new customer, plus some profit, within 30 days (source: FounderOS — designing-money-models)
evidence: Work out how many $2-profit sales pay back a $6 cost to win a customer
Turn sales into days: if a customer buys once a day, how many days until they pay back
Check whether a plan passes the 30-day payback rule and suggest a change if it does not
topics.assessmentPrompt: If it cost {{name}} $10 in free samples to win a new snack customer who brings $2 profit a week, could they work out the payback period and say whether it passes the 30-day rule?

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: The offer ladder
topics.description: A money model is a planned sequence of offers, not a random pile of products: attract (a first offer that wins new customers), upsell (a bigger or better offer for those who said yes), downsell (a smaller or cheaper option for those who said no) and continuity (something that repeats, like a weekly snack box); the take rate is the percent of customers who say yes, and extra cash per customer = take rate × the offer's profit (source: FounderOS — designing-money-models)
evidence: Design a four-step offer ladder (attract, upsell, downsell, continuity) for a lemonade stand
Work out the extra cash from 20 customers when 25% of them take a $2 upsell
Explain why a downsell means a customer's 'no' is not the end of the sale
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} offered a cookie with every lemonade and 40% of 30 customers said yes, could they work out how much extra cash the upsell brought in?

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Price testing
topics.description: Finding a good price by testing: start lower, raise the price in steps, and use a price × number sold table (minus costs) to find the total profit at each step; keep raising while total profit goes up, and when total profit drops, step back one price (source: FounderOS — designing-money-models)
evidence: Fill in a price × number sold table and find the total profit at each price
Pick the best price from a table where profit rises and then falls, and explain why the highest price is not always best
Explain the rule: keep raising the price until total profit goes down, then step back one
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sold 40 drinks at $1, 30 at $2 and 15 at $3, with each drink costing 50¢ to make, could they find which price earns the most profit?

topics.subject: Life Skills
topics.name: Billing math
topics.description: The maths of repeat payments: prices are often shown in the smallest unit ('$5 a day') and billed over a longer cycle (a month, a term, a year), so check the total; billing every 28 days instead of once a month makes 13 payments a year instead of 12, about 8.3% more (1 ÷ 12); an honest seller makes the yearly total clear (source: FounderOS — designing-money-models)
evidence: Turn a price per day into a price per week, month and year
Show that billing every 28 days gives 13 payments a year and work out how much more that is than 12 monthly payments
Compare paying monthly with paying for a whole year up front, and explain why a fair seller shows the yearly total
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a snack club cost $5 every 28 days, could {{name}} work out the total for a year and explain why it is more than $5 a month for 12 months?
